Welcome to lesson eighteen: tags, and keeping versions! Real projects keep versions, so if version two has a bug, you can go back to version one. You do that with tags.
Before we start, why do we need versions?
In lesson seventeen, you built with dash t, my site. Every rebuild replaced the previous one, and you only had my site, latest.
In this lesson, you'll use name colon tag, like my site, tag v one, and my site, tag v two. Then if version two has a bug, version one is still there.
A tag is the part after the colon in name colon tag. You first saw it in lesson one.
Step one. Let's build version one.
First, go to your my site folder from lesson seventeen. You've used this command before. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
C D, my site. You're in the project folder.
Now replace the page's text with a heading that says, Version one. You've used this command before. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
echo, the Version one heading in single quotes, into index dot H T M L.
Now build it, this time with a tag after the name: docker build, dash t, my site colon v one, dot. Docker finishes with, naming to my site, v one.
Look closely. My site is the name, and v one is the tag, joined by a colon.
And a tag can be anything you like: v one, one point oh, or even a date.

echo, the Version two heading, into index dot H T M L. The page file is updated.

docker build, dash t, my site colon v two, dot. And look: my site v one and my site v two are both kept!

Two versions, running at the same time. If version two had a bug, version one is right there. Just run my site, v one, again. That's called a rollback.
Step five. Here's a surprise about latest. Look at the list from step three again.
V two is your newest build. But latest has a different I D. It's still the old image from lesson seventeen!
So latest does not mean newest. It's only the tag Docker uses when you don't give one, and it doesn't move by itself.
So how do you move latest? Yourself, with docker tag. It gives an existing image another name.
docker tag, my site v two, my site latest. Watch the latest label move from the old image over to v two.
Let's check. List the my site images again. You've used this command before. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker image L S, my site. Now latest and v two have the same I D. It's one image with two names, and no copy was made.
The old latest lost its only name, so docker image L S no longer shows it. But it still uses disk space. If you like, delete it with docker image R M and its I D from step three. Use your own I D.

Great job! You can now version your images. docker build with name colon tag builds a version. docker run with name colon tag runs a specific version. docker tag gives an existing image another name, with the same I D. And remember, latest is just the default tag, not the newest. Next, in lesson nineteen, you'll package your own program. See you there!
